summary_and_theme.summary: Rabindranath Tagore's poignant poem 'Vocation' captures the innocent mind of a school-going child observing various street workers. At 10 AM, he meets a hawker selling glass bangles. At 4 PM, coming back from school, he observes a gardener digging soil, getting dusty, and working freely without anyone scolding him. At night, through his bedroom window, he watches the lonely night watchman swinging his lantern and walking with his shadow. Envying their apparent freedom from rigid routines, strict adult rules, and early bedtimes, the child longs to become a hawker, a gardener, and a watchman.
summary_and_theme.core_theme: Childhood innocence, dignity of labor, desire for freedom, and imaginative empathy for community helpers.

reading_extracts.extract:
The lane is dark and lonely, and the street-lamp stands like a giant with one red eye in its head.
The watchman swings his lantern and walks with his shadow at his side, and never once goes to bed in his life.
I wish I were a watchman walking the streets all night, chasing the shadows with my lantern.

writing_prompts.topic: Write a diary entry as the child narrator reflecting on why you wish for the freedom of the gardener and watchman.
writing_prompts.model_answer:
23rd September 2026
Dear Diary,
Today on my way back from school, I saw the gardener digging the flowerbed. His clothes were covered in dirt, yet no one scolded him or forced him to take a bath. At night, while I was sent to bed early, I looked out my window and saw the watchman walking freely with his lantern. I wish I could be like them—free from rigid schedules and able to spend my time outdoors under the open sky!
- Ankit

short_answer.question: Why does the child narrator envy the hawker, gardener, and watchman?
short_answer.answer: The child envies them because he perceives them as having complete freedom—no fixed timetable, no strict adult discipline, no scolding for getting dirty, and no compulsory bedtime.

short_answer.question: Explain the simile used to describe the street-lamp in 'Vocation'.
short_answer.answer: Tagore compares the street-lamp to a 'giant with one red eye in its head', creating a vivid image of a tall, solitary glowing red lamp standing guard in the dark lane.

long_answer.question: How does Rabindranath Tagore portray childhood innocence and the dignity of labor in the poem 'Vocation'?
long_answer.answer: In 'Vocation', Tagore brilliantly captures the innocent perspective of a young schoolboy. Unaware of the hardships and physical toll of manual labor, the child sees only the romanticized freedom enjoyed by street workers. When he watches the hawker, he admires the absence of fixed hurry; when he sees the gardener, he envies playing in soil without reprimand; when he observes the watchman, he longs to stay awake chasing shadows. Simultaneously, the poem honors the dignity of labor by presenting these humble community workers—hawkers, gardeners, and watchmen—as figures of fascination and respect, proving that every honest job holds intrinsic value.
